title: Kraków Main Market Square shooting: six killed; prosecutors treat it as terrorism
seoTitle: Kraków shooting: six killed in the Main Market Square
dek: A gunman shot people at random on Kraków's Main Market Square on 7 November, killing six and wounding at least 15, including two police officers. Three of his relatives were found dead at his home. He died in hospital on 9 November; prosecutors are treating it as a terrorist offence.
happened: At about 15:00 on Saturday, 7 November, a man drove a car onto Kraków's Main Market Square and fired at people at random, then kept shooting as he drove through the city centre. Police pursued him and stopped him on Dietla Street after an exchange of fire, wounding and detaining him. Six people were killed, four women and two men; a British citizen and an Austrian citizen are among them. At least 15 were injured, including two police officers who were seriously wounded while stopping him. Police said he used a semi-automatic rifle similar to the American AR-15, and more weapons were found in the car. He is a 24-year-old Polish citizen from Ostrowiec Świętokrzyski who held a sport-shooting permit and had no criminal record. At his home there, police found three more people dead, two women and a man; Radio Kraków reports police identified them as his parents and sister. France 24 calls it Poland's deadliest shooting since the fall of communism in 1989. The attacker died in hospital on 9 November from wounds sustained in the shootout with police. Prosecutors are treating the attack as a terrorist offence.

sides.says: Prime Minister Donald Tusk called the attack an act of "terrorism", announced national mourning and said: "Our highest praise goes to the heroic police officers who risked their lives in the line of duty." He asked that the tragedy not be used for political disputes. Interior Minister Marcin Kierwiński said the suspect appeared to be "fascinated by far-right ideologies" and held "ultra-nationalist views", and that "everything suggests that the perpetrator held very, very radical views"; he described this as an initial analysis that still needs to be verified.

He said he was awaiting "a full explanation of the circumstances surrounding these dramatic events" and that "the safety of Poles is an absolute priority". Radio Kraków reports he plans to honour the police officers for bravery.

Mayor Łukasz Gibała praised the city guards, who followed the attacker without firearms, and the police. He urged residents to stay calm and not to share unverified information or graphic footage, and said the city will remain open and welcoming. The city declared mourning until 11 November. Gibała said the city will not bury the attacker at public expense; if relatives do not arrange a funeral, the body will go to the Jagiellonian University's medical college.

Prosecutors are treating the attack as a terrorist offence and are handling the Kraków killings and the three deaths at the attacker's home as one case. The justice minister said there were "very strong traces of right-wing extremism" in the attacker's online activity. Police denied early reports that a second attacker was being sought, and investigators are checking whether anyone helped him; no confirmed motive has been published.

Deputy Defence Minister Magdalena Sobkowiak-Czarnecka said firearm access rules, including limits on how many guns one person can own, should be discussed. Police figures cited by France 24 show more than 50,000 new firearms licences issued in 2025, for 411,000 in total.

A mass for the attacker and his dead relatives was held there on 16 November. The parish said it was "a private initiative of one of the priests, not of St Mary's Parish", that praying for the dead "in no way indicates justification for the crime", and it rejected any "trivialisation of the suffering of the victims". The family asked the media to "respect the privacy, dignity and mourning of our family and loved ones".

next: The two police officers wounded in the shootout had emergency surgery and were recovering in hospital, Notes From Poland reported on 16 November. The investigation into the attack and the deaths at the attacker's home continues; no gun-law changes have been announced.
summary: On 7 November a gunman drove onto Kraków's Main Market Square and shot people at random, killing six, among them a British and an Austrian citizen, and wounding at least 15, including two police officers who stopped him. Three of his relatives were found dead at his home. He died in hospital on 9 November. Prosecutors are treating it as terrorism, and the government says he appeared to hold far-right views; the investigation continues.
